disease_info: Specific Phobia is characterized by marked, persistent fear or anxiety focused on a clearly circumscribed object or situation (e.g., animals, heights, flying, injections) that is out of proportion to the actual threat posed. Exposure to the phobic trigger almost invariably elicits an immediate anxiety response and leads to active avoidance or intense distress when avoidance is impossible, causing clinically significant interference in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning. The course is often chronic if untreated, with onset typically in childhood or early adulthood, though new phobias can emerge later in life after stressful or traumatic experiences. It is distinguished from other anxiety disorders by its narrow focus on a specific stimulus rather than generalized worry, social evaluation, or unexpected panic attacks across many contexts.

narrative.stressor: About a year ago, Tacy fell after becoming light‑headed during routine blood work at her primary care clinic, which led to a minor wrist fracture and several weeks of reduced independence. Since then, her physicians have recommended more frequent lab monitoring for her age‑related conditions, but each scheduled blood draw has become a major ordeal, complicating her ability to manage her health and increasing reliance on neighbors and her adult son for accompaniment. Her usual methodical planning has turned into elaborate efforts to reschedule or work around appointments, disrupting her walking club routine and volunteer commitments at the senior center. When she finally canceled a much‑anticipated cataract surgery solely because it required pre‑operative labs, her son insisted she speak with a mental health professional about how this fear was undermining her medical care.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Any time I have to get blood drawn, I go to great lengths to avoid it or sit there in sheer terror the whole time.”

narrative.stressor: Eleven months ago, on an early‑morning surf session, Keith was caught in a sudden rip current that pulled him far from shore before a lifeguard reached him, an incident that shook his long‑held sense of safety in the ocean central to his Polynesian identity. At first he told himself he just needed a break, but he began turning down friends’ invitations to surf, backing out of planned trips to Maui, and even avoiding walking near the water after work, despite living minutes from the beach. The shift started to clash with his social life, his role in community cultural events that revolve around the ocean, and his own self‑image as a water‑person, fueling tension between his careful planning and impulsive efforts to distract himself with gaming or extra shifts at the shop. When he found himself unable to join a family ceremony held at the shoreline, staying in the parking lot instead, his uncle suggested he get professional help because his fear of the ocean was starting to control major parts of his life.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I’ve developed this intense, irrational fear of going into the ocean, even though I grew up surfing.”

narrative.stressor: Around eleven months ago, Linda was rotated to a new crew tasked with high‑rise renovation work that required frequent use of open‑frame scaffolding and lifts, a step up from the single‑story projects she was used to. She initially tried to push through but began quietly trading tasks to avoid being assigned to upper levels, which started to undermine her informal leadership role and drew criticism from a foreman who had been mentoring her toward a promotion and NCCER certification. Her avoidance led to missed overtime, friction with coworkers who felt she wasn’t pulling her weight on certain jobs, and growing worry that she wouldn’t qualify for the supervisory positions she’d been working toward. The turning point came when she skipped a mandatory skills assessment that involved working on a training tower, and her union rep suggested she see a mental health provider after she admitted that just knowing she might have to be up high was enough to keep her from showing up.
narrative.chief_complaint: “As soon as I know I have to go up high on a building, I get an overwhelming rush of fear the moment I even approach the scaffolding.”
